training.prompt: Hold the definition before the topics
training.script: Do not start with a pile of topics. First psychology courses throw dreams, vision, and personality at you. Hold one sentence instead. Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior. Psyche means life. Logos means explanation. MIT and OpenStax open with that same sentence. Examples come after, as proof. A grid that flashes dots that are not printed. An attention bottleneck. Thoughts that run without a meeting. Those examples defend the definition. They are not a replacement for it. The live debates stay open on purpose.

blocks.heading: One sentence
blocks.body: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior. Psyche is life. Logos is explanation.

blocks.heading: Examples are proof
blocks.body: Illusions, attention limits, and automaticity come after the definition. They defend it. They are not the definition.

blocks.heading: Debates stay open
blocks.body: Nature and nurture, free will, consciousness. A first course does not close these. It teaches you to ask them with evidence.

teaching.prompt: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior
teaching.script: Psychology is not a vibe check. It is the scientific study of how we think, feel, and act. MIT's introduction course calls it a survey of human nature: how the mind works, and how the brain supports the mind. OpenStax uses the same core sentence. Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior. The Greek roots are psyche, meaning life, and logos, meaning explanation. Hold that definition. Everything else in a first course hangs off it. Yale's open course with Paul Bloom walks in through everyday questions. What do dreams mean. Why you cannot tickle yourself. How people decide, remember, love, and get persuaded. Same science. Different door. Here is the analogy. Your mind is not a camera. It is a construction crew. Optical illusions are the proof they use on day one at MIT. In the Hermann grid, black dots seem to flash in the crossings. The dots are not on the page. Your visual system invented them. Attention is a bottleneck. You do not see everything in front of you. You see what the system selected. That is why a move can hide in plain sight. Automaticity is the next heading. A lot of thinking, feeling, and acting runs without a meeting. That speed is useful. It is also the peril. You can be sure, and still be constructed. Last split: how we feel versus how we act. They can come apart. Psychology treats that split as data, not as a moral fail. The live debates in this course are nature and nurture, free will, consciousness, human differences, self and society. You do not settle them in five minutes. You learn to ask them with evidence.

blocks.heading: The definition
blocks.body: Start here. Do not skip to topics.

blocks.heading: What the field is
blocks.body: Psychology is the scientific study of how we think, feel, and act — a survey of human nature: how the mind works, and how the brain supports the mind.

blocks.heading: Mind and behavior
blocks.body: OpenStax: psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior. Psyche is life. Logos is explanation.

blocks.heading: The door Yale uses
blocks.body: Bloom's course asks ordinary questions on purpose: dreams, tickling yourself, persuasion, love, hunger, fiction. The science is the same as MIT's survey. The hook is daily life.

blocks.heading: Not a camera
blocks.body: The mind is a construction crew. The Hermann grid makes black dots flash in the crossings. The dots are not printed. Perception built them.

blocks.heading: Attention and automaticity
blocks.body: Two limits of the construction crew.

blocks.heading: Attention is a bottleneck
blocks.body: You do not see the whole scene. You see what got selected. Limits of visual attention are a first-lecture demo for a reason.

blocks.heading: Automaticity
blocks.body: Much of thinking, feeling, and acting runs without a meeting. Speed is the power. Unchecked certainty is the peril.

blocks.heading: Feel versus act
blocks.body: How we feel and how we act can split. A calm face is not a calm body. Treat the split as data.

blocks.heading: The debates you will keep meeting
blocks.body: Nature and nurture. Free will. Consciousness. Human differences. Self and society. First courses do not close these. They teach you to ask them with evidence.

checks.prompt: Which sentence is the core definition used in these open courses?
choices: Psychology is a set of tips for being happier
Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior
Psychology is only the study of mental illness
checks.expected: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior

checks.prompt: The Hermann grid is in lecture 1 to show what?
choices: That printed pages hide secret ink
That perception constructs what you see, it does not just record it
That attention can hold every detail at once
checks.expected: That perception constructs what you see, it does not just record it

checks.prompt: In two or three sentences: why is automaticity both useful and dangerous?
checks.expected: Automaticity lets thinking, feeling, and acting run without a meeting, which is fast and useful, but it can make you feel sure even when the mind constructed a wrong picture.
checks.rubric: Pass if they name a benefit (speed, no effort, runs without a meeting) AND a cost (unchecked certainty, constructed error, peril).

recognition.prompt: Which sentence is the core definition these open courses use for psychology?

options.text: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior
options.explanation: This is the exact definition MIT and OpenStax both open with. Psyche means life, logos means explanation.

options.text: Psychology is mostly about diagnosing mental illness
options.explanation: Clinical work is one branch. The field's own definition is broader: mind and behavior in general, not only disorder.

options.text: Psychology is a set of tips for a happier life
options.explanation: Self-help content borrows from psychology, but the field itself is a science with evidence and methods, not a tips list.

microCorrections.clinical_only: Clinical psychology studies disorder, but the field's core definition is wider: the scientific study of mind and behavior in general, healthy or not.
microCorrections.self_help: Self-help sometimes cites psychology, but the field is defined by its method, evidence and study, not by handing out life tips.

application.prompt: A news article says 'psychologists proved staring at a photo of your ex for 10 minutes cures heartbreak,' with no study cited. Applying the course's definition, what is the strongest reaction?

options.text: Ask what evidence and method back the claim, since psychology means scientific study, not folk wisdom
options.explanation: Right. The definition itself, scientific study of mind and behavior, is the test: no cited evidence, no real psychological claim.

options.text: Trust it, since it uses the word psychologist
options.explanation: Using the word does not make a claim scientific. The definition requires actual study behind it.

options.text: Reject it because it is about heartbreak, not real psychology
options.explanation: Emotion and relationships are legitimate psychology topics. The problem is missing evidence, not the topic.

generation.prompt: Explain to a 12-year-old what psychology actually studies, using your own example.
generation.coreIdea: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior, not just mental illness or self-help tips, but how people think, feel, and act, backed by evidence.

recognition.prompt: The Hermann grid (black dots seeming to flash at the crossings) is used in lecture 1 to show what?

options.text: That perception constructs what you see, it does not just record it
options.explanation: Correct — the dots are not printed. Your visual system builds them, which is the whole point of the demo.

options.text: That printed pages contain hidden ink
options.explanation: The dots are not physically on the page in any form, hidden or not. The point is that perception builds an experience, it is not a hidden-object puzzle.

options.text: That attention can hold every detail of a scene at once
options.explanation: This gets the lesson backwards. The grid is about perception constructing content, not about attention holding everything at once.

microCorrections.literal_illusion: The dots you see are not hidden on the page in any form. Your visual system generates them. The demo shows that perception constructs experience, not that it hides secrets.
microCorrections.attention_unlimited: The lecture's actual point about attention is that it is a bottleneck: you see only what got selected, not everything at once. The Hermann grid is about construction, not unlimited capacity.

application.prompt: You glance at a crowded room and instantly feel like something is 'off,' even though you can't say what changed. Which idea from the lecture best explains why your brain reacts before you can name the reason?

options.text: Perception actively constructs the scene, so a mismatch can register before conscious naming catches up
options.explanation: Right. Since perception is construction, not recording, a built mismatch can surface as a feeling before you can name it.

options.text: You must have a perfect memory of the room from before
options.explanation: The lecture's point is the opposite: memory and attention are limited, not perfect. That is not what explains the reaction.

options.text: It only means you are anxious
options.explanation: Possible in general, but it skips the course's actual concept: a built perception can flag a mismatch before you consciously identify it.

generation.prompt: Give a real example from your own life where what you perceived turned out to be your mind constructing something, not a direct recording.
generation.coreIdea: Perception is active construction, not passive recording, like the Hermann grid's phantom dots, so what you 'see' isn't a direct copy of the world.

training.prompt: Listen for the pairing, not the story
training.script: When you hear a lecture on learning, listen for the pairing, not the story. Classical conditioning: a neutral cue becomes a predictor. The tone starts to mean food. Operant conditioning: behavior that works gets more likely. The cat escapes faster. Generalization is leak. A fear of a white rat spreads to other white furry things. Discrimination is the split. This tone means food. A nearby tone does not. Pavlov and Little Albert are the vehicles. The pairing is the point.

blocks.heading: Two families
blocks.body: Classical: a cue becomes a predictor. Operant: a behavior that works gets more likely.

blocks.heading: Leak versus split
blocks.body: Generalization is leak to similar cues. Discrimination is the split: this cue, not that one.

blocks.heading: The stories are vehicles
blocks.body: Pavlov's dog and Little Albert carry the pairing. Do not stop at the story.

teaching.prompt: Learning is how experience changes what we do next
teaching.script: MIT's learning session asks two questions. How do we learn. How do the things we learn help us survive and deal with the environment. Start with classical conditioning. Pavlov's dog did not think about steak. A tone that used to mean nothing started to mean food, so saliva showed up before the food did. A neutral cue became a predictor. That is the concept. Operant conditioning is the other family. Thorndike's cat got out of the box faster each time a move was followed by escape. Behavior that works gets more likely. Behavior that fails gets less likely. Little Albert is the dark example in the same lecture: a learned fear can attach to a white rat, then leak toward other white furry things. That leak is generalization. A response shows up for cues that only resemble the original. Discrimination is the opposite skill. Pavlov's dog can learn: this exact tone means food. A nearby tone does not. MIT's check-yourself uses that split on purpose. Habituation is simpler still. Repeat a stimulus, and the reaction shrinks. A siren in a new city is huge. A week later it is furniture. Learned helplessness is what happens when nothing you do changes the outcome. The animal, or the person, stops trying even later, when a door is open. Delayed gratification is the other edge: a smaller now versus a larger later. The point of this module is not the famous names. It is the prediction. Learning is the system updating what comes next. If that sentence is still mush, ask. Then we check.

blocks.heading: The question
blocks.body: How do we learn, and how does that help us survive an environment.

blocks.heading: Learning
blocks.body: Experience changes what we do next. The lecture walks from classical conditioning to more complex models, including learned helplessness and delayed gratification.

blocks.heading: Classical conditioning
blocks.body: A neutral cue becomes a predictor. Pavlov: the tone starts to mean food, so saliva arrives before the food.

blocks.heading: Operant conditioning
blocks.body: A move that works becomes more likely. Thorndike's cat escapes faster because escape follows the right action.

blocks.heading: Little Albert
blocks.body: A learned fear can attach to a rat, then leak to other white furry things. That leak is the next heading.

blocks.heading: Generalization versus discrimination
blocks.body: Two predictions. Do not mix them.

blocks.heading: Generalization
blocks.body: Respond to cues that resemble the original. Similar situation, same predicted outcome.

blocks.heading: Discrimination
blocks.body: Treat a nearby cue as different enough. Similar is not the same. Different outcome.

blocks.heading: Habituation
blocks.body: Repeat a stimulus and the reaction shrinks. New siren, then furniture. That is not the same as choosing not to care.

blocks.heading: Learned helplessness
blocks.body: When nothing you do changes the outcome, trying can stop — even later, when a door is open. It is a failed prediction, stored.

checks.prompt: In Pavlov's setup, what did the dog actually learn?
A student is rude to one short-haired experimenter, then avoids a different person who only looks similar. That is closest to:
A person stops applying for jobs after months of silence, then ignores a real opening. Name the idea, and say what prediction got stored.
checks.expected: Learned helplessness: the stored prediction is that nothing I do changes the outcome, so trying is useless even when a door is open.
checks.rubric: Pass if they name learned helplessness (or a close paraphrase) and state that the person learned outcomes do not depend on their actions.

recognition.prompt: In Pavlov's setup, what did the dog actually learn?

options.text: That a tone predicts food
options.explanation: Right. The tone became a predictor of food, which is the whole mechanism of classical conditioning.

options.text: How to salivate on command like a trick
options.explanation: Salivating is a reflex, not a trained trick the dog performs on purpose. The dog learned an association, not a voluntary act.

options.text: That the tone itself contains food
options.explanation: The tone is just a signal, not a physical source of food. It becomes a predictor of food arriving, not food itself.

microCorrections.voluntary_trick: Salivation here is a reflex, an automatic response, not a trick the dog chooses to perform. Classical conditioning changes what triggers a reflex, not what the animal decides to do.
microCorrections.literal_association: The tone doesn't become food or contain it. It becomes a predictor, a signal that food is coming. That is the whole mechanism: a neutral cue starts to forecast an outcome.

application.prompt: A child feels nauseous every time they smell a specific cologne, because they once got very sick at a party where someone wore it. This is closest to:

options.text: Classical conditioning: a neutral cue, the smell, became linked to an unpleasant outcome, nausea
options.explanation: Right. A previously neutral cue got paired with an automatic reaction until it could trigger that reaction alone.

options.text: Operant conditioning: the child is being rewarded for avoiding the smell
options.explanation: Operant conditioning is about consequences following a chosen behavior. Here nothing was chosen: the smell got linked to an automatic reaction, which is classical conditioning.

options.text: Discrimination: the child learned to tell smells apart
options.explanation: Discrimination is about responding differently to similar cues. This example is one cue getting paired with a reaction, the conditioning itself, not the fine-tuning step.

generation.prompt: Give a real example of classical conditioning from your own life or work.
generation.coreIdea: Classical conditioning is when a neutral cue gets paired with an automatic response until the cue alone triggers that response, a predictor forms, not a chosen behavior.

recognition.prompt: Thorndike's cat got out of a puzzle box faster over repeated tries. What does that demonstrate?

options.text: Behavior that is followed by a good outcome becomes more likely
options.explanation: Right. Escape reinforced the move that produced it, so that move became more likely next time.

options.text: The cat memorized the exact box like a map
options.explanation: Thorndike's point wasn't a mental map. It was a move getting reinforced by its consequence, escape, so that move became more likely.

options.text: The cat is simply born knowing how to escape boxes
options.explanation: The behavior clearly improved with repetition, which rules out 'born knowing it.' A successful action got reinforced by its consequence.

microCorrections.cognitive_map: Thorndike's experiment isn't about the cat memorizing a layout. It's about a specific action getting reinforced because it was followed by escape, making that action more likely next time.
microCorrections.innate_skill: The behavior clearly improved with repetition, which rules out 'the cat was just born knowing it.' What changed is that a successful action got reinforced by its consequence.

application.prompt: A manager notices that employees who speak up in meetings get praised publicly, and now more employees are speaking up. This best illustrates:

options.text: Operant conditioning: a behavior, speaking up, is reinforced by a consequence, praise, so it increases
options.explanation: Right. A chosen behavior increased because it was followed by a reinforcing consequence.

options.text: Classical conditioning: the meeting itself has become a predictor of praise
options.explanation: Close, but the mechanism here is a chosen behavior being strengthened by its consequence, not a neutral cue becoming a predictor of an automatic reaction.

options.text: Generalization: employees are copying each other's tone of voice
options.explanation: The example is about a behavior increasing because of a consequence, not a response spreading to similar cues.

generation.prompt: What would go wrong if you didn't understand operant conditioning?
generation.coreIdea: Operant conditioning means behavior is shaped by its consequences: reinforced behavior increases, punished or ignored behavior decreases. Missing this, you might reward the wrong things by accident or miss why a behavior keeps happening.

modules.subject: computer-science
modules.title: A program is a named recipe

sources.title: 6.0001 Introduction to Computer Science and Programming in Python
sources.attribution: Guttag, John. 6.0001 Introduction to Computer Science and Programming in Python. MIT OpenCourseWare.

training.prompt: Listen for the recipe, not the language
training.script: MIT's intro CS is not a tour of Python. It is computational thinking: break a job into steps a machine can follow. Hold three objects while you listen. A variable is a labeled box. The name stays. The value can change. A conditional is a fork in the recipe. A loop is the same steps while a test is still true. The easy miss is the stop. If the value the test reads never changes, the loop never ends. A function is a named recipe you can call again. That is the stance. Next is one idea: a program is a named recipe.

blocks.heading: Python is the vehicle
blocks.body: MIT 6.0001 is computational thinking. The language is how the steps get written down, not the point.

blocks.heading: Three objects to hold
blocks.body: A box with a name. A fork in the recipe. A loop that must be able to stop.

blocks.heading: A miss is a step
blocks.body: Debugging is asking which step did not match what you thought. Not a verdict on you.

teaching.prompt: A program is a named recipe you can run
teaching.script: MIT's intro CS course is not a catalog of languages. It is computational thinking: break a job into steps a machine can follow. Hold that. A variable is a labeled box. The name stays. The value can change. x equals 3, then x equals x plus 1. The box named x now holds 4, not the text x plus 1. A conditional is a fork in the recipe. If the test is true, take this branch. If not, take the other. A loop is the same steps while a condition is still true. The easy miss is the stop. If the value the test reads never changes, the loop never ends. A function is a named recipe you can call again. You give it inputs, it does the steps, it can give a result back. Debugging is not shame. It is asking: which step did not match what I thought.

blocks.heading: The idea
blocks.body: Not a language. A way to write steps a machine can follow.

blocks.heading: Computational thinking
blocks.body: MIT 6.0001 starts here: break a job into precise steps. Python is the vehicle, not the point.

blocks.heading: Variable
blocks.body: A labeled box. The name stays. The value can change.

blocks.heading: x = 3, then x = x + 1
blocks.body: The box named x now holds 4. It does not hold the text “x + 1”.

blocks.heading: Conditional
blocks.body: A fork. If the test is true, take this branch. If not, take the other.

blocks.heading: Loop
blocks.body: The same steps while a condition is still true. If the value the test reads never changes, the loop never ends.

blocks.heading: Function
blocks.body: A named recipe. You call it, pass inputs, get a result. You do not rewrite the steps each time.

blocks.heading: A miss is a question
blocks.body: Debug means: which step did not match what I thought. Not: I am bad at this.

checks.prompt: x = 3 then x = x + 1. What is in the box named x?
A loop never stops. What is the usual miss?
choices: The variable name is too short
The stop condition never becomes true
checks.expected: The stop condition never becomes true

checks.prompt: In two sentences: what is a function, in this module’s terms?
checks.expected: A function is a named recipe you can call again. You give it inputs and it runs the same steps.
checks.rubric: Pass if they say it is a named set of steps you can reuse, not a loop or a variable.

recognition.prompt: x = 3 then x = x + 1. What is in the box named x?

options.explanation: Right. The right side is computed as math first, so x is reassigned to the number 4.

options.text: x + 1 as text
options.explanation: The right side of '=' is evaluated as math before being stored. The box holds the number 4, never the literal text 'x + 1'.

options.text: 3, unchanged
options.explanation: Assignment replaces the old value. The second line overwrites x with a new number, it doesn't leave the old 3 in place.

microCorrections.string_confusion: The right side of '=' is evaluated first, as math, before being stored. So x becomes the number 4, never the literal text 'x + 1'.
microCorrections.no_reassignment: Assigning to a variable replaces its old value. After 'x = x + 1', the box named x holds a new number, 4. The old 3 is gone.

application.prompt: You're tracking a running total of points in a game: total = 0, then every time a player scores you run total = total + points. After scores of 5, 3, and 2, what's the core reason this pattern works?

options.text: Each run reads the current value in the box, adds to it, then overwrites the box with the new value
options.explanation: Right. The variable holds one current value; each step reads it, adds, then overwrites it.

options.text: The variable remembers every past value it ever held
options.explanation: A variable only holds its current value, it doesn't keep a history. The pattern works because each step reads then overwrites.

options.text: The program recalculates all three scores from scratch every time you check total
options.explanation: There's no recalculation from the original scores. Each step just updates the single stored value, which is why the variable pattern is efficient.

generation.prompt: Explain to a 12-year-old what a variable is, using your own example.
generation.coreIdea: A variable is a named, labeled box that holds one value at a time. The name stays the same, but the value inside can be replaced by reassignment.

recognition.prompt: A recipe says: 'If the oven is preheated, put the tray in. Otherwise, wait 5 minutes.' Which idea from the lesson does this map to?

options.text: A conditional, a fork in the recipe based on a test
options.explanation: Right. It's a one-time yes/no fork, which is exactly what a conditional is.

options.text: A loop, the same steps repeating until a test is true
options.explanation: There's no repetition here. This is a one-time fork, do A or do B, which is a conditional, not a loop.

options.text: A function, a named set of steps you can call again
options.explanation: There's no reusable named recipe being called here. This is a single yes/no branch, which is a conditional, not a function.

microCorrections.loop_confusion: A loop repeats the same steps while a condition stays true. This recipe step only branches once, preheated or not, with no repetition, so it's a conditional, not a loop.
microCorrections.function_confusion: A function is a reusable named set of steps you call again and again. This is a single one-time fork in the recipe, which is exactly what a conditional is.

application.prompt: A program should charge a customer full price if they have no coupon, and a discounted price if they do. What is the simplest correct way to describe this in the course's terms?

options.text: A conditional: if a coupon is present, take the discount branch, otherwise take the full-price branch
options.explanation: Right. The program checks once and picks one of two branches, which is exactly a conditional.

options.text: A loop that keeps checking coupons until one works
options.explanation: Nothing here repeats. The program checks the coupon once and picks a branch, which is a conditional, not a loop.

options.text: A variable that stores the final price directly
options.explanation: A variable can hold the final price, but the decision of which price to use is made by a conditional fork, not by the variable itself.

generation.prompt: Give a real example of a conditional, an if / otherwise fork, from your own life or work.
generation.coreIdea: A conditional is a fork in the steps: if a test is true, take one branch, if not, take the other. It picks between paths, it does not repeat steps.
